title: The third boon: does a man exist after death?
theme: Naciketas asks his third boon: there is doubt about a man who has died — some say he is, some say he is not; taught by you, I would know this.

words.context: Śaṅkara: «प्रेते मृते»; Raṅgarāmānuja, with the Śrībhāṣya: one released from all bonds

sandhi.rule: e before a is left unjoined (see the junction below); i before a dissimilar vowel becomes y, P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि).
a + a → ā, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः); i + i → ī, the same rule; a + e → ai, P. 6.1.88 (वृद्धिरेचि).
t before v becomes d, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते); visarga before t becomes s, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः); ā + a → ā, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः).

sandhi.type: eṣaḥ before a consonant; visarga before t
sandhi.rule: eṣaḥ loses its visarga before a consonant, P. 6.1.132 (एतत्तदोः सुलोपोऽकोरनञ्समासे हलि); visarga before t becomes s, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः).

sandhi_exceptions.note: manuṣye asti: final e before a is not joined (no avagraha); the text keeps the two words apart, as the witnesses do.

morphology.note: A desiderative noun from cit ‘perceive’: ‘wishing to discern’, hence doubt.
Optative 1 sg. of vid ‘know’ (vidyām), ‘may I know’ — not the noun vidyā.
Past participle of pra-i ‘go forth, depart’: the dead. The Śrībhāṣya, as Raṅgarāmānuja reports, takes it as released from all bonds.

translation.literal: ‘This doubt which [exists] concerning a man who has departed — “He is,” some [say], and “He is not,” some — this may I know, taught by you. Of the boons this is the third boon.’
translation.readable: ‘When a man dies there is this doubt: some say he still exists, others say he does not. Teach me, and let me know the truth of it. That is my third wish.’

syntax: A relative clause (yeyaṃ prete vicikitsā manuṣye) defines the subject, quoted with the two views (astīty eke, nāyam astīti caike). The main clause etad vidyām anuśiṣṭas tvayāham states the wish, and varāṇām eṣa varas tṛtīyaḥ closes it formally.

ambiguities.topic: What is the doubt about — survival after death, or release?
ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: whether there is a self, distinct from body, senses, mind and intellect, that is connected with another body: «अस्ति शरीरेन्द्रियमनोबुद्धिव्यतिरिक्तो देहान्तरसम्बन्ध्यात्मा इत्येके मन्यन्ते». Raṅgarāmānuja, reporting the Śrībhāṣya: the question is not about bodily death but about the released state, «न शरीरवियोगमात्राभिप्रायम् अपि तु सर्वबन्धविनिर्मोक्षाभिप्रायम्». Madhva: about the Lord present as controller in the released, «प्रेते मुक्ते मनुष्ये नियामकत्वेन भगवानस्तीति ज्ञानिनो वदन्ति».
Madhva’s text reads vṛtaḥ, ‘chosen’, for varaḥ, ‘boon’ (corrections.json).

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: Counted as written, 22 and 21 syllables: the second line (etad vidyām anuśiṣṭas tvayāhaṃ varāṇām eṣa varas tṛtīyaḥ) is one syllable short; Vedic metre often allows a short pāda.

beginner: This is the question the whole Upaniṣad answers. When a person dies, Naciketas says, people disagree: some say he still exists, some say he does not. Teach me the truth, he asks; that is my third wish. It is the oldest question there is, and the boy asks it of Death himself. The commentators agree that this is the turning point: the first two wishes were about family and ritual, this one is about what we really are. Śaṅkara notes that neither perception nor reasoning can settle it, so it must be taught.
analogy: Like asking the one person who has seen the other side of a locked door to say what is there.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: Whether a man who has died still exists: some say he does, some that he does not. He asks Death to teach him the truth, as the third boon.

commentary.q: Why is this the turning point?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: what the first two boons point to can be known from the ritual portion of the Veda, but not the true nature of the self: «नात्मतत्त्वविषययाथात्म्यविज्ञानम्». So the rest of the Upaniṣad teaches the knowledge of the one Brahman-self that ends ignorance. Neither perception nor inference can decide the question: «अत्र चास्माकं न प्रत्यक्षेण नाप्यनुमानेन निर्णयविज्ञानम्».

commentary.q: What is the doubt about, for Raṅgarāmānuja?
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: He reports the Śrībhāṣya (on Brahmasūtra 1.2.9): the question concerns release, «न शरीरवियोगमात्राभिप्रायम् अपि तु सर्वबन्धविनिर्मोक्षाभिप्रायम्», and lists rival views of release — annihilation, the end of ignorance, a stone-like isolation, the self’s merging into the Supreme — against the Vedānta of the Lord’s qualified unity.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: ‘The departed man’ is the released soul: the wise say the Lord is there as its controller, the ignorant that he is not: «प्रेते मुक्ते मनुष्ये नियामकत्वेन भगवानस्तीति ज्ञानिनो वदन्ति । नास्तीत्यज्ञाः». Madhva argues from the answer the Upaniṣad later gives, «एतद्वै तत्», that the question is about the Lord in the released: «मुक्ते स्थितो भगवान् पृच्छ्यते इति सिद्धम्».

advaita.text: The question is whether a self exists beyond body and mind: «अस्ति शरीरेन्द्रियमनोबुद्धिव्यतिरिक्तो देहान्तरसम्बन्ध्यात्मा». The answer, unfolded in the rest of the Upaniṣad, is the self’s identity with Brahman, which only teaching can give.

visistadvaita.text: The doubt concerns the nature of the released self, not mere survival: «न शरीरवियोगमात्राभिप्रायम् अपि तु सर्वबन्धविनिर्मोक्षाभिप्रायम्». Release is the self’s natural experience of the Supreme, of whom it is the body.

dvaita.text: The third boon is knowledge of the Lord who abides as controller in the released soul: «तस्य नियामकस्य स्वरूपं यथावदहं विद्याम्».

schools.disagreement: What the doubt is about is itself disputed. Śaṅkara: the existence of a self beyond the body. The Śrībhāṣya (via Raṅgarāmānuja): the nature of the released self. Madhva: the Lord in the released self. All agree that the answer must be taught, not inferred.

parallels.note: Yājñavalkya’s ‘after death there is no awareness’ is the kind of statement that makes people say ‘he is not’; the Śrībhāṣya, as Raṅgarāmānuja reports it, cites the same words in explaining this question.
The Gītā’s answer to the same doubt — the self is not slain when the body is slain — is close in words to the Kaṭha’s own answer at 1.2.18.

contemporary.text: Whether anything of a person continues after death is still the question people bring to every tradition, and to science. Naciketas asks it plainly and refuses easier gifts. The Upaniṣad treats the asking as the beginning of wisdom. (A modern reflection.)

reflect.beginner: What do you think happens to a person after death — and why do you think so?
reflect.deeper: Why would perception and reasoning be unable to settle this question?
reflect.practice: Sit quietly for five minutes and ask yourself, without answering: ‘What in me would remain?’

references.text: Raṅgarāmānuja cites the Śrībhāṣya on Brahmasūtra 1.2.9 and 1.4.6 and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka; Madhva cites the Tattvasāra and the Brahmāṇḍa by name. These are reported as cited by them.

flags.note: Whether the doubt concerns the self’s survival of death (Śaṅkara), the nature of release (Śrībhāṣya, via Raṅgarāmānuja) or the Lord in the released (Madhva) shapes how the rest of the Upaniṣad is read.
Madhva’s text reads vṛtaḥ for varaḥ; the vishvAsa mūla writes manuṣye ’sti with an avagraha (spelling) (corrections.json).
